title: Chapter 5 — Your Personal Operating System
intro: The daily and weekly structure that turns a sales job into a sales business.

sections.title: You Are a Business Inside a Business
sections.content:
Whether you realize it or not, you are running a small business inside a larger one. You have a pipeline, a customer base, a revenue target, and a reputation. The store gives you a floor, products, and a name on the door. Everything else — your income, your growth, your career trajectory — depends on how well you run your personal operation.

The reps who treat this like a job show up, wait for customers, and go home. The reps who treat it like a business have systems. They have a morning routine. They have a follow-up cadence. They have a pipeline they review every day. They have a CRM that is current, not three weeks behind.

The difference between $60,000 and $120,000 per year is not talent. It is operating discipline.

sections.title: The Daily Five
sections.content:
Every day, before anything else, make five intentional outbound contacts. Not reactive. Not responding to walk-ins. Five proactive touches that YOU initiate.

One follow-up on an open quote — highest priority because it is closest to revenue. One post-delivery check-in — this builds referrals and reviews. One past customer touch — 12 or more months out, stay top of mind. One new prospect — builder, designer, property manager, referral lead. One value-add to anyone — send an article, a product update, a promo alert.

Five is achievable. It takes 20-30 minutes. It compounds. Over a month, that is 100 touches. Over a year, 1,200. Most appliance salespeople make zero proactive contacts per day. You will have 1,200 more conversations than they did.

Do it before 11am. Do not wait until the afternoon when the floor gets busy. The Daily Five is a morning habit, like coffee.

sections.title: The Weekly Review
sections.content:
Every Friday or Sunday, spend 20 minutes reviewing your week. Not the store's week — YOUR week.

How many ups did you take? How many did you close? What is your close rate this week? Look at your open quotes — how many are still live? Which ones need a follow-up call on Monday? Check your delivery schedule — who is getting delivered next week and needs a post-delivery call?

Review your CRM pipeline. Move stale deals. Update notes. Clean up contacts. A messy CRM is like a messy desk — it slows everything down and makes you miss opportunities.

The weekly review takes 20 minutes and it is the single most productive 20 minutes of your week. It sets up Monday so you start the week with a plan instead of a blank stare.

sections.title: Time Management on the Floor
sections.content:
The highest-earning reps do not work more hours. They spend more of their hours on activities that produce revenue.

Green time is revenue-producing: greeting customers, presenting products, demoing, closing, following up on quotes, making Daily Five calls. Target 70 percent or more of your floor time here. Yellow time is revenue-supporting: learning product knowledge, organizing your pipeline, prepping quotes, team meetings. Target 20 percent. Red time is revenue-killing: scrolling your phone, extended break room sessions, complaining about traffic, hiding in the warehouse. Target zero.

When the floor is empty, that is not break time. That is your time to follow up on open quotes, update CRM notes, learn a new product, practice a demo, call past customers, and prep for the next walk-in. Reps who use dead time productively outsell reps who wait for traffic by 40-60 percent.

sections.title: Your Personal Scorecard
sections.content:
Track these numbers weekly. Not because your manager asks — because you need them.

Revenue. Close rate — sales divided by qualified ups. Average ticket. Attach rate. Follow-up conversion — how many quoted customers came back and bought. Daily Five completion. Training progress.

Trends matter more than individual data points. If your close rate dropped from 28 percent to 22 percent this month, something changed. Was it your discovery? Your demo? Your close? The data tells you where to focus.

The rep who knows their numbers controls their income. The rep who does not is hoping. Hope is not a strategy.
